Colleagues remembered Johns as a friendly presence at the museum’s doors, someone who greeted visitors with kindness and treated coworkers like family. In the aftermath of the shooting, fellow security officers wept openly, embraced one another and struggled to describe the pain of losing a man they had stood beside day after day.

“He was one of us,” many said in the hours after the attack, as flowers and messages of condolence began to gather near the museum.

The shooting occurred at a museum dedicated to preserving the memory of the Holocaust and warning against hatred and antisemitism. Officials identified the suspect as an elderly man with a history of extremist and antisemitic views. He was wounded when officers fired back and was taken into custody.

Museum officials praised the security team’s courage, saying Johns and the officers who responded acted with extraordinary bravery under sudden and terrifying circumstances. Law enforcement authorities said the rapid response likely saved lives.

Johns’ death turned the museum itself into a place of mourning. Visitors, staff members and officers who had spent years protecting the building found themselves confronting violence rooted in the kind of hatred the museum exists to document and oppose.

In statements following the attack, officials honored Johns as a hero. His fellow officers, however, remembered him not only for how he died, but for how he lived — as a dependable coworker, a proud father and a kind man whose absence was immediately felt.

For those who stood watch with him, the grief was visible and raw. They had trained to protect the museum and its visitors, and on that day they did. But they also lost a friend.
